title: Topic 6.5 Q55/Q56 Bernoulli stagnation and reservoir teacher-decision proposals
provenance: Prepared-master compiled question pp.189–190 and original answer key p.195 were previously source-checked; printed NBF pp.99–100 supports Bernoulli formula, not verbatim candidate question wording.

candidates.originalStem: If ideal horizontal water slows from 4 m/s to 0 m/s, by how much does static pressure increase?
candidates.proposedStem: In steady ideal horizontal flow, water of density 1000 kg/m³ moves at 4 m/s at point X and reaches a stagnation point Y (local speed 0 m/s) along the same streamline. Neglect viscous losses. By how much is the static pressure at Y greater than at X?
candidates.proposedExplanation: Along a horizontal, lossless streamline ending at a stagnation point, P_Y − P_X = ½ρ(v_X² − v_Y²) = ½(1000)(4² − 0²) = 8000 Pa = 8 kPa. The original answer B is correct when the zero-speed condition is local stagnation, not zero discharge everywhere.
candidates.whyClarify: The original describes slowing from 4 to 0 m/s without identifying the zero-speed location. A stagnation point has zero local speed while steady throughflow can continue around the body; zero average velocity across an entire unbranched downstream pipe section would contradict steady incompressible continuity.
workedPhysics: Choose point X in the moving flow, v_X = 4 m/s, and stagnation point Y, v_Y = 0 m/s.
The points are on the same level ideal streamline, so P_X + ½ρv_X² = P_Y + ½ρv_Y².
With ρ = 1000 kg/m³, P_Y − P_X = 0.5 × 1000 × 16 Pa = 8000 Pa = 8 kPa.
The static-pressure increase is 8 kPa: original source letter B.
modelLimitations: Zero local velocity at a stagnation point is physically different from stopping all fluid discharge through a complete pipe section.
The ideal, horizontal, same-streamline assumptions and explicit density make the calculation determinate; they do not certify an individual FBISE exam item.

candidates.issue: Large-reservoir nearly-zero inlet speed versus finite-section rest
candidates.originalStem: Ideal horizontal water accelerates from rest to 10 m/s. If upstream pressure is 100 kPa, the downstream pressure is:
candidates.originalExplanation: The kinetic term rises by ½(1000)(10²) = 50 kPa, so pressure falls to 50 kPa.
candidates.proposedStem: Water of density 1000 kg/m³ flows steadily from a very large reservoir into a horizontal duct. At point X in the reservoir, its speed is negligible and its static pressure is 100 kPa. At point Y downstream on the same elevation and streamline, the water speed is 10 m/s. Neglect viscous losses and pumps. What is the static pressure at Y?
candidates.proposedExplanation: Apply ideal horizontal Bernoulli between a near-stagnant point in a very large reservoir and a downstream point on the same streamline. P_Y = P_X + ½ρ(v_X² − v_Y²) ≈ 100000 + ½(1000)(0 − 10²) Pa = 50000 Pa = 50 kPa. The original letter B is retained. No downstream atmospheric discharge is assumed.
candidates.whyClarify: The original phrase 'accelerates from rest to 10 m/s' in steady ideal flow can be misunderstood as a finite upstream throughflow section with zero discharge. A very large reservoir makes the initial local speed negligibly small while finite flow can pass through the smaller duct. No open-to-atmosphere outlet boundary is inferred.
workedPhysics: In a large reservoir the local approach speed at X is negligible compared with the downstream duct speed, so v_X ≈ 0.
The ideal same-elevation streamline relation gives P_Y = P_X + ½ρ(v_X² − v_Y²).
With ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and v_Y = 10 m/s, dynamic pressure rise is 50000 Pa = 50 kPa.
The downstream static pressure is 100 kPa − 50 kPa = 50 kPa: original letter B.
modelLimitations: A zero-speed finite inlet cross section cannot supply positive downstream discharge in steady, incompressible, unbranched throughflow.
The calculated downstream pressure is a point in a duct and is not asserted to be an atmospheric-pressure free-jet exit; the source alone does not specify that boundary.
Any nonnegligible head loss, pump, elevation change or initial reservoir speed would require further model terms.
